source_refs.note: Book p. 79: 5.1.1 Proper Rational Fraction (definition and three examples). The degree table, Teaching note, Exam tip, Key points and Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: A rational function \(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) is called a Proper Rational Fraction if the degree of the polynomial \(P(x)\) in the numerator is less than the degree of the polynomial \(Q(x)\) in the denominator.
For example, \(\frac{3}{x+1}\), \(\frac{2x-5}{x^{2}+4}\) and \(\frac{9x^{2}}{x^{3}-1}\) are proper rational fractions or proper fractions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
To decide, find two numbers and compare them: the degree (highest power of \(x\)) of the numerator and of the denominator. The size of the coefficients does not matter.
The table below does this for the book's three examples. Notice the first one: the numerator \(3\) is a constant, and a non-zero constant has degree 0, because \(3 = 3x^{0}\).

blocks.caption: Checking the book's three proper fractions

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
When the denominator is given as a product, its degree is the sum of the degrees of its factors: \((x+1)(x-2)\) has degree \(1 + 1 = 2\), and \((x-1)^{2}(x+3)\) has degree \(2 + 1 = 3\). You do not need to multiply it out.
Always check "proper or not?" first. Only a proper fraction can be split into partial fractions directly; this is step (i) of the method in 5.1.3.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) is proper when degree of \(P(x)\) < degree of \(Q(x)\).
2. Degree = highest power of \(x\); a non-zero constant has degree 0.
3. Degree of a product = sum of the degrees of the factors.
4. Proper fractions are resolved into partial fractions directly.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Comparing coefficients instead of powers: \(\frac{9x^{2}}{x^{3}-1}\) is proper although \(9 > 1\); only the powers 2 and 3 count.
2. Comparing the number of terms: \(\frac{2x-5}{x^{2}+4}\) has two terms on top and two below, yet it is proper (\(1 < 2\)).
3. Reading the degree of \((x+1)(x-2)\) as 1: a product of two linear factors has degree 2.
